title: Fixed-Boost Wigner Noise: Strict Trace-Distance Contraction without Quantum Degradability
abstract: A Lorentz boost acts on the canonical spin of a massive particle through a momentum-dependent Wigner rotation. We show that, for one fixed observer boost, reducing over an uncertain momentum can strictly contract every pairwise spin-state trace distance without producing a channel that is degradable from the less contracted one. For spin $1/2$, we first characterize the exact inversion-symmetric channel cone generated by a fixed Wigner angle and transverse momentum directions. Inside this cone lies the Pauli family $M_α=\operatorname{diag}(1-α,1-α,1-2α)$, $0\leqα<1/2$. For $0<α<β<1/2$, all trace distances between distinct spin states are strictly smaller after $M_β$ than after $M_α$, yet the unique linear post-processing factor has a negative normalized Choi eigenvalue. We solve the optimization over all physical converters exactly: $\frac{1}{2}\inf_{Λ\in\mathrm{CPTP}}\|Φ_β-Λ\circΦ_α\|_\diamond=\frac{α(β-α)}{2-3α}$, whereas the reverse deficiency is $β-α$. Thus the identity dominates the family, while all positive-noise members are pairwise incomparable under CPTP post-processing. The ideal construction is realized as the narrow-packet limit of pure, normalizable five-component momentum states, and explicit perturbation and finite-shot tomography bounds certify an open set of examples. Separately, every nonidentity member fails embedding in a time-homogeneous Pauli-diagonal Lindblad semigroup. Hence ordering all unassisted spin distinguishabilities does not determine the quantum statistical post-processing order.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the noise introduced to particle spin states by a fixed Lorentz boost. It demonstrates that even when all pairwise distinguishabilities decrease monotonically, this reduction cannot be modeled by a single, universal quantum channel (CPTP map). This shows that local measures of information loss are insufficient for characterizing global quantum processing constraints.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether strict contraction of pairwise spin-state trace distance under a fixed Lorentz boost implies the existence of a state-independent quantum channel that performs this reduction.
main_result: It proves a counterexample showing that while all pairwise spin contrasts can decrease after a fixed boost, no single CPTP map exists to account for this reduction, meaning ordering distinguishabilities does not determine post-processing order.
method: The analysis uses mathematical characterizations of channel cones (for spin 1/2), deriving explicit formulas for operational gaps ($\delta_\diamond$), and constructing counterexamples based on the failure of unique factor criteria.
model_or_system: The system models massive particles undergoing Lorentz boosts, with spin states analyzed via Wigner rotations. The noise is characterized by fixed-boost channels acting on spin qubits (Pauli mixtures).
key_observables: Pairwise spin-state trace distance ($\|\cdot\|_1$), normalized Choi eigenvalues ($\lambda_{\min}$), and the directed CPTP deficiency ($\delta_\diamond$).
important_parameters: The boost parameters defining the source ($u$) and target ($v$) channels, and perturbation sizes ($\epsilon$ or $\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to an 'autonomous product preparation' of spin and momentum states; counterexamples are constructed for fixed boosts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that the target contrasts can fall below source contrasts, accompanied by negative Choi eigenvalues, demonstrating non-degradability. Other figures plot the exact directed CPTP deficiency on the Pauli line.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (Lorentz boosts and spin noise) to characterizing the resulting channel cone structure. It then constructs a concrete counterexample using specific weights ($u, v$) and derives quantitative measures for the operational gap ($\delta_\diamond$), concluding with theorems showing violations of Pauli-Markovian semigroup embedding.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous mathematical constraints on how quantum information degrades under relativistic kinematics, offering insights into fundamental limitations that go beyond simple componentwise damping assumptions.
